title: Meeting people and daily life
intro: Introduce yourself, talk about your day and use the past tense correctly.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.intro: The first two minutes of any conversation. Learn these and you will sound confident.

phrases.en: Hi, I'm Kwame. Nice to meet you.
phrases.note: Use your own name. Say "Nice to meet you" only the first time you meet someone.
A friendly way to start a conversation.

phrases.en: I'm from Ghana, but I live in Leeds now.

phrases.note: This means "What is your job?", not "What are you doing now?"
Say "I work in" + an industry, or "I'm a/an" + a job: I'm an engineer.

phrases.en: How long have you lived here?
phrases.note: Use the present perfect for something that started in the past and is still true.
A polite way to end the conversation.

lessons.tip: British people often say "Alright?" as a greeting. It means "Hello, how are you?" Answer "Yeah, good thanks, you?"

dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Sam. I don't think we've met.
Hi Sam, I'm Kwame. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you too. Where are you from?
I'm from Ghana, but I've lived in Leeds for two years.
Oh, nice! And what do you do?
I work in a warehouse. What about you?

lessons.title: Talking about your day
lessons.intro: Describe your routine with the present simple: I wake up, he goes, they work.

phrases.en: I usually get up at six o'clock.
I have breakfast and then I go to work.
phrases.note: We say "have breakfast", not "eat breakfast", most of the time.

phrases.en: My wife takes our son to school.
phrases.note: he / she / it: add -s to the verb: takes, goes, works.

phrases.en: I finish work at half past five.
phrases.note: half past five = 5:30. quarter to six = 5:45.

phrases.en: In the evening, I relax and watch TV.
phrases.note: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening, but at night.

phrases.en: At the weekend, I go to church and see friends.
phrases.note: British English says "at the weekend". American English says "on the weekend".

lessons.tip: Frequency words go before most verbs but after "be": I always walk to work. I am always tired on Monday.

lessons.title: What did you do yesterday?
lessons.intro: Use the past simple for finished actions. Many common verbs are irregular.

phrases.en: Yesterday I went to the supermarket.
I drove my son to school this morning.
phrases.note: drive → drove. "this morning" is finished, so use the past.

phrases.en: We had dinner with some friends.
I bought a new phone last week.
Did you watch the match on Saturday?
phrases.note: Questions: Did + subject + base verb. Not "Did you watched".

phrases.en: No, I didn't. I was too tired.
phrases.note: Negative: didn't + base verb. be → was / were.

lessons.tip: Listen for -ed endings. "worked" sounds like "workt", "played" sounds like "playd", and "wanted" has an extra syllable: "want-id".

cards.meaning: A person you work with.
cards.example: My colleague helped me with the report.

cards.meaning: A person who lives next to you or near you.
cards.example: Our neighbours are very friendly.

cards.meaning: To travel to and from work every day.
cards.example: I commute by bus. It takes 40 minutes.

cards.meaning: To get out of bed.
cards.example: I get up at six on weekdays.

cards.meaning: To have a good, friendly relationship with someone.
cards.example: I get on well with my manager.

cards.meaning: Having a lot to do.
cards.example: I'm really busy this week.

cards.meaning: Needing rest or sleep.
cards.example: I was tired after the long shift.

cards.meaning: To change from a child into an adult.
cards.example: I grew up in Accra.

cards.meaning: The town or city where you were born or grew up.
cards.example: My hometown is near the coast.

cards.meaning: Most of the time; normally.
cards.example: I usually cook dinner at seven.

cards.meaning: Not often.
cards.example: I rarely eat fast food.

cards.meaning: To feel happy about something that will happen.
cards.example: I'm looking forward to the weekend.

cards.meaning: To talk in a friendly, informal way.
cards.example: We had a quick chat after church.

cards.meaning: A little; slightly.
cards.example: I'm a bit cold. Can you close the window?

cards.meaning: British: thank you, or goodbye. Also said when drinking together.
cards.example: Cheers for your help!

cards.meaning: To fix or organise something.
cards.example: I need to sort out my bank account.

cards.meaning: A fixed time to meet someone, like a doctor.
cards.example: I have a doctor's appointment at ten.

cards.meaning: To be later than planned.
cards.example: Sorry, I'm running a bit late.

cards.meaning: Monday to Friday.
cards.example: The shop is open until eight on weekdays.

cards.meaning: British: to want or like the idea of something.
cards.example: Do you fancy a cup of tea?

quiz.q: She ___ to work by bus every day.
quiz.explain: With he / she / it in the present simple, add -s: she goes.
Use the present perfect with "since" for something that started in the past and continues now.

quiz.q: Yesterday I ___ my son to school.
___ you watch the match on Saturday?
quiz.explain: Past simple question: Did + subject + base verb.

options: I always am tired on Monday.
I am always tired on Monday.
Always I am tired on Monday.
quiz.explain: Frequency words go after the verb "be": I am always…
"What do you do?" is the common way to ask about someone's job.

quiz.q: In the UK, people often say ___ the weekend.
quiz.explain: British English: at the weekend. American English: on the weekend.

quiz.q: "I get on well with my manager" means…
options: I have a good relationship with my manager.
I work more than my manager.
quiz.explain: To get on (well) with someone = to have a friendly relationship.

speak.text: Hi, nice to meet you. I'm from Ghana, but I live in Leeds now.
I usually get up at six o'clock and have breakfast.
My wife takes our son to school in the morning.
I finish work at half past five.
speak.note: "half past" is often said quickly: "haaf paast".

speak.text: Yesterday I went to the supermarket and bought some bread.
Did you watch the match on Saturday?
I'm really looking forward to the weekend.
Sorry, I'm running a bit late. I'll be there in ten minutes.

questions.q: Tell me a little about yourself.
tips: Say where you are from and where you live now.
questions.model: I'm originally from Ghana, but I've lived in Leeds for about two years. I work in a warehouse, and I'm learning English to get a better job. In my free time I like playing football and cooking.

questions.q: What does a normal day look like for you?
tips: Use time words: first, then, after that, in the evening.
questions.model: I usually get up at six and have a quick breakfast. Then I take the bus to work, which takes about forty minutes. I finish at half past five, and in the evening I cook dinner and relax with my family.

questions.q: What did you do last weekend?
tips: Use the past simple: went, had, saw, bought.
Say who you were with and how it was.
questions.model: On Saturday I went shopping in the city centre with my wife. In the evening we had dinner with some friends. On Sunday I went to church and then I relaxed at home. It was a nice, quiet weekend.
